      <content name="title">Hip Injuries and Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">Pelvis</span></span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Your hip is the joint where your femur (thigh bone) meets your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">pelvis</span></span> (hip bone). There are two main parts: a ball at the end of the femur, which fits in a socket in the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">pelvis</span></span>. Your hip is known as a ball-and-socket joint. This is because you have a ball at the end of your femur, and it fits into a socket in your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">pelvis</span></span>. This makes your hips very stable and allows for a wide range of motion. When they are healthy, it takes great force to hurt them. However, playing sports, running, overuse, or falling can sometimes lead to hip injuries such as:</p><ul><li>Strains</li><li>Bursitis</li><li>Dislocations</li><li>Fractures (broken bones)</li></ul><p>Certain diseases also lead to hip injuries or problems. Osteoarthritis can cause pain 
and limited motion. Osteoporosis of the hip causes weak bones that break easily. Both of 
these are common in older people.</p><p>Another problem is hip dysplasia, where the ball at the end of the femur is loose in the hip socket. It can cause hip dislocation. Babies who have hip dysplasia are usually born with it, but sometimes they develop it later.</p><p>Treatment for hip disorders may include rest, medicines, physical therapy, or surgery, including hip replacement.  </p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/bladdercancer.html">
      <content name="title">Bladder Cancer</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Urinary Bladder Cancer</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>The bladder is a hollow organ in your lower abdomen that stores urine. Bladder cancer occurs in the lining of the bladder. It is the sixth most common type of cancer in the United States.</p><p>Symptoms include:</p><ul><li>Blood in your urine</li><li>A frequent urge to urinate</li><li>Pain when you urinate</li><li>Low back pain</li></ul><p>Risk factors for developing bladder cancer include smoking and exposure to certain chemicals in the workplace.  People with a family history of bladder cancer or who are older, White, or male have a higher risk.</p><p>Treatments for bladder cancer include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and biologic therapy. Biologic therapy boosts your body's own ability to fight cancer.</p><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/kidneycancer.html">
      <content name="title">Kidney Cancer</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Hypernephroma</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Renal Cancer</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>You have two kidneys. They are fist-sized organs on either side of your backbone above your waist. The tubes inside filter and clean your blood, taking out waste products and making urine.  Kidney cancer forms in the lining of tiny tubes inside your kidneys. </p><p>Kidney cancer becomes more likely as you age. Risk factors include smoking, having certain genetic conditions, and misusing pain medicines for a long time.</p><p>You may have no symptoms at first. They may appear as the cancer grows. See your health care provider if you notice:</p><ul><li>Blood in your urine</li><li>A lump in your abdomen</li><li>Weight loss for no reason</li><li>Pain in your side that does not go away</li><li>Loss of appetite</li></ul><p>Tests to diagnose kidney cancer include blood, urine, and imaging tests. You may also have a biopsy.</p><p>Treatment depends on your age, your overall health and how advanced the cancer is. It might include surgery, chemotherapy, or radiation, biologic, or targeted therapies.  Biologic therapy boosts your body's own ability to fight cancer. Targeted therapy uses drugs or other substances that attack specific cancer cells with less harm to normal cells.</p><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/ovariandisorders.html">
      <content name="title">Ovarian Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Ovarian Insufficiency</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are ovaries?<p>The ovaries are a pair of female reproductive glands that make eggs and female hormones. Women have one ovary on each side of the uterus (where a fetus grows during pregnancy). Each ovary is about the size and shape of an almond.</p><p>Ovaries play a role in menstruation, pregnancy, and menopause.  Your ovaries:</p><ul><li>Produce and store eggs that are released during ovulation (when an egg leaves the ovary and travels into the fallopian tube). If a sperm fertilizes the egg, you can become pregnant.</li><li>Make the female hormones estrogen and progesterone.</li><li>Stop making those hormones and releasing eggs during menopause.</li></ul><p>Some medical problems can affect the ovaries. These can cause various symptoms, and some ovarian disorders may need prompt treatment.</p>What are the types of ovarian disorders?<p>Some problems that can happen with the ovaries can include:</p><ul><li>Ovarian cancer is when a cancerous tumor forms in the tissues of an ovary.</li><li>Ovarian cysts are fluid-filled sacs in or on an ovary.</li><li>Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a set of symptoms related to an imbalance of hormones.</li><li>Primary ovarian insufficiency is when your ovaries stop working before age 40.</li><li>Ovarian torsion is a twisting of the ovary.</li><li>Endometriosis is when tissue like the lining in your uterus grows in other places in your body. It may affect the ovaries, fallopian tubes, and tissue lining the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">pelvis</span></span>.</li><li><span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">Pelvic</span></span> inflammatory disease is an infection and inflammation of the uterus, ovaries, and other female reproductive organs.</li><li>Ovarian tumors.</li></ul>What causes ovarian disorders?<p>Ovarian disorders can happen for different reasons depending on the condition. Sometimes the cause is unknown.</p>What are the symptoms of ovarian disorders?<p>Your symptoms may be different, depending on the problem with your ovaries. Some ovarian disorders, such as ovarian cysts, may cause few or even no symptoms. Other disorders may cause more severe symptoms. Symptoms can include:</p><ul><li><span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">Pelvic</span></span> pain, which often happens during your period</li><li>Nausea or diarrhea</li><li>Vaginal bleeding that is between periods, very heavy, or longer than usual</li><li>Vaginal discharge</li><li>Painful menstrual cramps</li></ul>How are ovarian disorders diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have a problem with your ovaries, your health care provider:</p><ul><li>Will ask about your medical history, including your symptoms</li><li>Will ask about your family health history</li><li>Will do a physical exam, including a <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">pelvic</span></span> exam</li><li>May order imaging tests, or blood tests</li></ul>What are the treatments for ovarian disorders?<p>Treatment depends on the ovarian disorder, your symptoms, overall health, and plans for pregnancy. Treatment can include medicines, such as pain relievers or hormonal birth control, lifestyle changes to reduce symptoms, or sometimes surgery. Ovarian cancer may require surgery, chemotherapy, or other targeted therapy.</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/pelvicfloordisorders.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">Pelvic</span></span> Floor Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cystocele</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Uterine Prolapse</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Enterocele</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">Pelvic</span></span> prolapse</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Rectocele</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>The <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">pelvic</span></span> floor is a group of muscles and other tissues that form a sling or hammock across the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">pelvis</span></span>. In women, it holds the uterus, bladder, bowel, and other <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">pelvic</span></span> organs in place so that they can work properly.  The <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">pelvic</span></span> floor can become weak or be injured. The main causes are pregnancy and childbirth. Other causes include being overweight, radiation treatment, surgery, and getting older.</p><p>Common symptoms include:</p><ul><li>Feeling heaviness, fullness, pulling, or aching in the vagina. It gets worse by the end of the day or during a bowel movement.</li><li>Seeing or feeling a "bulge" or "something coming out" of the vagina</li><li>Having a hard time starting to urinate or emptying the bladder completely</li><li>Having frequent urinary tract infections</li><li>Leaking urine when you cough, laugh, or exercise</li><li>Feeling an urgent or frequent need to urinate</li><li>Feeling pain while urinating</li><li>Leaking stool or having a hard time controlling gas</li><li>Being constipated</li><li>Having a hard time making it to the bathroom in time</li></ul><p>Your health care provider diagnoses the problem with a physical exam, a <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">pelvic</span></span> exam, or special tests. Treatments include special <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">pelvic</span></span> muscle exercises called Kegel exercises. A mechanical support device called a pessary helps some women. Surgery and medicines are other treatments.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Child Health and Human Development</p></content>
